17.3 Amines

Amines are important nitrogen containing organic compounds. These are the derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by one or more similar or different alkyl groups (or aryl groups).

On the basis of the number of alkyl or aryl groups directly bonded to nitrogen atom, amines have been classified into primary, secondary and tertiary amines shown below.

17.3.1 Nomenclature

Amines are named by common and IUPAC systems.

a. Common system

Common names of amines are formed from the names of the alkyl groups bonded to nitrogen, followed by the suffix -amine.

The prefixes di- and tri- are used to describe two and three identical substituents, attached to nitrogen.

If different alkyl groups are attached to the nitrogen, then they are named separately in alphabetical order.

b. IUPAC system

In IUPAC nomenclature of amines, the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms determines the root name. The -e ending in the alkane name is changed to suffix -amine and a number shows the position of the amino group along the chain. Other substituents on the carbon chain are given numbers, and the prefix N- is used for each substituent on nitrogen.

Tidbit

Amines also possess metamerism. For example, ethyl methyl amine and trimethyl amine are metamers of each other.

17.3.2 Physical Properties

Low molecular weight amines are generally gases or low boiling liquids at room temperature. They possess a characteristic ammonia like smell.

Amines have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar molecular weight due to the presence of intermolecular hydrogen bondings. The molecules of primary and secondary amines have high boiling points because they are able to form hydrogen bondings among their molecules.

Molecules of tertiary amines cannot form hydrogen bonding among themselves, thus having lower boiling points than primary and secondary amines of the same molecular weight.

However, all lower primary, secondary and tertiary amines can form hydrogen bonding with water and therefore lower amines are soluble in water.

This method is particularly used for conversion of alkyl halides to carboxylic acids. The resulting carboxylic acids contain a carbon more than parent alkyl halide.

17.3 Amines

Amines are important nitrogen containing organic compounds. These are the derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by one or more similar or different alkyl groups (or aryl groups).

On the basis of the number of alkyl or aryl groups directly bonded to nitrogen atom, amines have been classified into primary, secondary and tertiary amines shown below.

17.3.1 Nomenclature

Amines are named by common and IUPAC systems.

a. Common system

Common names of amines are formed from the names of the alkyl groups bonded to nitrogen, followed by the suffix -amine.

The prefixes di- and tri- are used to describe two and three identical substituents, attached to nitrogen.

If different alkyl groups are attached to the nitrogen, then they are named separately in alphabetical order.

b. IUPAC system

In IUPAC nomenclature of amines, the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms determines the root name. The -e ending in the alkane name is changed to suffix -amine and a number shows the position of the amino group along the chain. Other substituents on the carbon chain are given numbers, and the prefix N- is used for each substituent on nitrogen.

Tidbit

Amines also possess metamerism. For example, ethyl methyl amine and trimethyl amine are metamers of each other.

17.3.2 Physical Properties

Low molecular weight amines are generally gases or low boiling liquids at room temperature. They possess a characteristic ammonia like smell.

Amines have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar molecular weight due to the presence of intermolecular hydrogen bondings. The molecules of primary and secondary amines have high boiling points because they are able to form hydrogen bondings among their molecules.

Molecules of tertiary amines cannot form hydrogen bonding among themselves, thus having lower boiling points than primary and secondary amines of the same molecular weight.

However, all lower primary, secondary and tertiary amines can form hydrogen bonding with water and therefore lower amines are soluble in water.
